rewrites.summary:
No Jalisco-specific statutes, votes, lethality figures or incident records are supported by the vetted sources for this record. The national framework is what governs: by March 2025 an international human-rights organization counted 22 of Mexico's 32 states as having legislated legal gender-recognition procedures, with six state legislatures enacting none, and a March 2024 report from the same organization documents that where no procedure exists, trans people face police stops, denied documents and institutional mistreatment.

For a visitor, Jalisco's own documented record is thin: expect the country-wide picture rather than verified local protections or verified local hostility.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Transfeminicide has become a criminal category in some states - the capital imposes up to 70 years - against more than 95% homicide impunity nationally, and reporting finds convictions lag the statutes; this policy trend is national and does not move Jalisco-specific risk either way.
rewrites.localsOnly: The national framework report documents the resident-side consequence where no procedure exists: identity-document mismatch driving discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with the documented incidents recorded in other states. No resident-facing data specific to Jalisco - registry practice, local surveys or resident discrimination statistics - is documented in the vetted sources.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Jalisco's own position in the national count is not named in the dossier - whether the state has legislated any recognition procedure is unresolved from these sources. No border-screening or document-procedure information specific to Jalisco is documented here, and no state-specific incident or lethality figures exist to verify.

rewrites.summary:
Nayarit was the first of Mexico's 32 states to criminalise transfeminicide, introducing sentences of up to 60 years in early 2024, and its law also lets friends, not only relatives, claim bodies and drive investigations - a provision that matters where families disown trans relatives. Because that statute landed against more than 95% impunity for homicides in the country in 2022, believed higher for transfeminicides, it records official posture more than proven protection.

On documents: a 2017 reform of the local Civil Code established an administrative legal-gender-recognition procedure allowing adults to change identity documents to match gender identity, so a trans visitor with documents issued in Nayarit can rely on a recognition route. No other Nayarit-specific incidents, enforcement records, border-screening practice or marriage/partner-travel information is supported by the vetted sources.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The parent-country frame: by March 2025 an international human-rights organization counted 22 of Mexico's 32 states as having legislated legal gender-recognition procedures, eight with none enacted and two more running one in practice. The capital followed Nayarit in July 2024 with its own transfeminicide statute of up to 70 years - the 'Paola Buenrostro law' - named for a trans sex worker murdered in 2016 whose attacker was released after 48 hours despite footage and witnesses and has not been caught since.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing: the 2017 civil-code recognition procedure is the operative identity-document practice for trans residents; the provision letting friends claim bodies matters where families disown trans relatives, a resident reality the law expressly addresses. No further resident discrimination or lethality data specific to Nayarit is documented in the vetted sources.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The transfeminicide statute's enforcement is unverified against any documented case, so the record reads it as official posture rather than demonstrated protection. No border-screening or document-procedure information specific to Nayarit is documented here, and no marriage/partner-travel information is recorded.

rewrites.summary:
For a visitor, the operative reading is a split local posture: Querétaro's congress banned conversion practices on 29 June 2023 with penalties of 2-6 years in prison plus fines and community service, yet the March 2025 state-by-state table of an international human-rights organization records that the state has not reformed its legislation to create any legal gender-recognition procedure, leaving trans people's identity documents permanently mismatched.

Where no procedure exists, mismatched documents expose trans people to police stops and institutional mistreatment; no state-specific incident or enforcement evidence was identified, so the visitor-relevant signal is the climate of the recognition refusal rather than any documented enforcement event.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The parent-country frame: by March 2025 an international human-rights organization counted 22 of Mexico's 32 states as having legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure, leaving this state among the never-legislating minority. The conversion-practices ban is characterized as discriminatory and torturous under articles 1 and 6 of the regional convention against torture, and local campaigners call it a milestone compared with states where a ban has been approved but remains unpublished.
rewrites.localsOnly: The absence of a recognition procedure is a resident-documentation issue; its visitor relevance is the climate signal of the refusal. Trans residents' identity documents remain permanently mismatched, and campaigners note that a first generation of LGBTIQ+ legislative reforms is still pending in the state.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Two of the four vetted sources were not retrievable at fetch time (no cached copy), so the national count and the documentation of mistreatment where no procedure exists rest on the citation of the dossier. No state-specific incident or enforcement evidence was identified, so the record is a legal-posture record without operational data.

No region-specific incident, enforcement or ordinance evidence was found, and no border-screening or document-procedure information specific to the state is recorded in the dossier.

rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing: the hate-crime statute of the state recognizes motivation by gender and sexual preference, and its local anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation and gender but not gender identity - a protection gap that leaves gender identity outside the explicit anti-discrimination text.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: One of the two vetted sources was not retrievable at fetch time (no cached copy), so the national count rests on the citation of the dossier. rewrites.summary:

Marriage is the firmer ground: the top national court ordered the state to legalize same-sex marriage within 90 days on 15 May 2018, and the state congress passed a same-sex marriage law on 15 June 2021, with civil unions for both same-sex and opposite-sex couples performed in the state. For a visitor, Sonora is at the protection-positive end of the national map: its congress approved a Gender Identity Law on 1 October 2020 under which people who identify with the opposite gender can modify their official documentation, and the state subsequently banned conversion practices on 6 December 2022. Same-sex marriage had been legalized in every Mexican state by 31 December 2022 - in Sonora by legislation, executive order or judicial ruling - so partner travel here is not a legal barrier.

The hate-crime laws of the state recognize motivation by gender and sexual preference, and no Sonora-specific incident or enforcement pattern is documented in the dossier; the protective reading rests on statutes rather than enforcement data, with no verified local hostility recorded either.

rewrites.summary:
Tabasco has enacted no legal procedure for recognising gender identity, and a dedicated report of an international human-rights organization (March 2024, co-produced with a local inclusion centre) documented that the absence of any recognition procedure leaves trans people's identity documents permanently mismatched and exposed to police and institutional mistreatment.

For a visible trans visitor the document mismatch is the practical trigger: an ID that does not match presentation invites the questioning and mistreatment the report records. No border-screening or document-procedure information specific to Tabasco is recorded in the dossier.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The parent-country frame: by March 2025 an international human-rights organization counted 22 of Mexico's 32 states as having legislated legal gender recognition, naming eight - among them Tabasco - whose legislatures have enacted none, with two more running a procedure in practice only; where no procedure exists, mismatched documents invite police stops and institutional mistreatment.

rewrites.summary:
For a visitor, the state's position is no-recognition: as of early 2026 no legal gender-recognition procedure exists, so identity documents issued in Tamaulipas cannot be changed through any administrative route, and mismatched documents invite exactly the police checks and institutional mistreatment that a companion 2024 report documents in one such state - the daily-interaction risk that most endangers a visible trans visitor.

On protections, the congress of the state unanimously approved, on 18 June 2025, reforms to the local Penal Code adding a chapter covering crimes against sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression and explicitly banning 'conversion therapies', with prison terms of 2-6 years and fines of up to 2,000 times a local measurement unit; the penalties increase by half when victims are minors, disabled or elderly, or in family, medical or workplace settings. For practical safety, the documented armed-group targeting and extortion of trans women along the border is the trans-specific danger driver, against blanket border violence that affects every traveller regardless of gender expression.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The parent-country frame: per the March 2025 count of 22 of 32 states as having legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure, this state is among the six whose legislatures have enacted none; where no procedure exists, mismatched documents invite the police checks and institutional mistreatment documented in a companion 2024 report on one such state.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing: as of early 2026 no legal gender-recognition procedure exists in the state, and the initiatives for a Gender Identity Law - pending since June 2025 - remain unpassed, with deputies and LGBT+ civil-society groups agreeing on 4 February 2026 a joint agenda for identity, anti-discrimination and health reforms; the absent law continues to limit trans people's access to health, education and employment.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Blanket armed-group violence along the border affects every traveller regardless of gender expression; the trans-specific element is the documented targeting and extortion of trans women by those same actors, which the assessment covers - a claim carried from the record's prior assessment, since none of the four vetted sources here documents it directly. The source summaries disagree on the never-legislating count - one names six, the state-by-state table places the state among eight with no procedure at all - and the record keeps the earlier 'six' wording. One of the four vetted sources was not retrievable at fetch time (no cached copy).

blindSourceSummaries: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time; the underlying source is a country overview of an international human-rights organization (31 March 2025) on transgender rights progress and challenges in the nation, headlining that 22 of the 32 state/province in the nation had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure by that date and naming six whose legislatures had enacted none.

A state/province-by-state/province table of an international human-rights organization (31 March 2025) records that this state/province 'has not reformed its legislation to create a legal gender recognition procedure for transgender people', placing it among the eight state/provinces with no procedure at all, against 22 of the 32 state/province in the nation that have legislated an administrative procedure (two more have one in practice only). For a trans person whose documents are issued in this state/province, this means there is no administrative route to change identity documents to match their gender identity.

On 18 June 2025 the congress of this state/province unanimously approved reforms to the local Penal Code adding a chapter on crimes against sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression, explicitly banning 'conversion therapies' with prison terms of 2-6 years and fines of up to 2,000 measurement units; penalties rise by half when victims are minors, disabled or elderly, or in subordinate settings such as family, medical or workplace. Dated evidence that the criminal law of this state/province protects gender identity even though the state/province still lacks an administrative gender-recognition procedure.

On 4 February 2026 deputies of the state/province legislature and LGBT+ civil-society groups agreed a joint agenda to push a Gender Identity Law and anti-discrimination and health reforms, noting the initiatives have been pending since June 2025 and that the absent law keeps limiting trans people's access to health, education and employment. Confirms that as of early 2026 no legal gender-recognition procedure exists in this state/province and a Gender Identity Law remains unpassed.
